threads.thread_goal: Align on scope, touchpoints, and overall pilot plan.

messages.text: Hi team, welcome to the Cross-Channel Customer Feedback Improvement Pilot kickoff. Over the next 30 days, we're going to design and run a pilot to capture, route, and act on customer feedback across digital, support, and membership channels. The goal is to understand how feedback flows today and build a process that works across all our teams. We'll be working with existing systems and tools, so we need to be pragmatic about what's possible. Let's start by mapping out which touchpoints we want to include in scope—help desk, membership interactions, cellar visits, and insurance complaints. I've started a process map in A1 and we'll need to document all current channels and owners. Looking forward to your input on what we should focus on first.

Thanks for the overview. From the membership side, we're definitely in scope—we interact with members through email, phone, and in-person at events. I'm thinking we should capture feedback at renewal touchpoints and after member events. One question: are we including feedback from our website contact forms, or is that handled by help desk?

Good question. Help desk currently handles web forms, phone support, and email tickets. We log them in our system but there's no consistent tagging across channels. That's part of what we're trying to fix. I think for the pilot we should include all of those, but we need to be realistic about what we can capture without slowing down our response times. I'm concerned about adding extra steps to our intake process.

From cellar operations, we do get feedback during vineyard tours and tastings. Right now it's informal—visitors mention things and staff remember or jot notes. For the pilot, we could use a simple checklist during tours, but we need to keep it brief. Peak season is coming up and we can't add complexity to the visitor experience. I'd suggest we limit feedback collection to specific time windows during tours.

Insurance side: we handle complaints through our ticketing system and we have complaint codes already. Those should map into whatever taxonomy we build. We get complaints about coverage, claims processing, and policy questions. I can help align our codes with the new structure once it's defined.

Thanks for that context. So to clarify scope: we're including help desk (web, phone, email), membership (email, phone, events), cellar visits (structured checklist during tours), and insurance complaints (existing system). That covers our main customer touchpoints. For the timeline, we need to move fast—30 days total. I'm thinking: Week 1 finalize taxonomy and scripts, Week 2-3 train teams and start pilot, Week 4 collect and analyze, Week 5 prepare report. Does that feel doable?

Timeline looks tight but I think we can make it work if we parallelize. I can start on the membership communication piece and training materials while you finalize the taxonomy. One thing I want to flag: we'll need to tell members we're collecting feedback and explain how we'll use it. That's part of the customer communication plan.

I can have a draft help desk script ready by end of week. I'll need to test it on a few recent tickets to make sure it doesn't slow us down. Also, we need to be clear on data privacy—what can we ask, how long we keep it, who can see it. That's critical for customer trust.

Agreed on privacy. I'll work with you on the data protection rules—we need to document access levels and retention periods. Insurance has strict requirements around complaint data, so we need to make sure the new process complies.

Perfect. So to confirm our scope decision: we're moving forward with help desk, membership, cellar visits, and insurance as our four main channels. Timeline is 30 days with Week 1 focused on taxonomy and scripts. I'll document this in A1 and we'll use it as our baseline. Next thread will be the taxonomy itself—I'll post a first draft by tomorrow EOD.

threads.thread_goal: Define and finalise the unified feedback taxonomy and routing rules.

messages.text: Here's my first draft of the feedback taxonomy for the pilot. I've grouped feedback into 15 categories: Product Quality, Delivery/Logistics, Customer Service, Membership Benefits, Insurance Coverage, Claims Processing, Website/Digital, Billing, Safety/Compliance, Staff Behavior, Facility/Cellar Experience, Pricing, Suggestions/Ideas, Complaints, and Other. Each category has 2-3 tagging examples. The idea is that every piece of feedback gets tagged with one primary category and optionally a secondary tag. I've documented this in A2. I need input from each team on whether these categories make sense for your workflows and if we're missing anything.

This looks pretty comprehensive. From membership, I'd say we see a lot of 'Membership Benefits' and 'Pricing' feedback, plus some 'Suggestions/Ideas' about events. One thing I'm not sure about: should we separate 'Complaints' from the other categories, or is that just a tag we add? Also, do we need a category for feedback about the feedback process itself?

Insurance side: we definitely see 'Claims Processing', 'Insurance Coverage', and 'Billing'. I notice you have 'Complaints' as a category—for us, most of what we handle is already a complaint by definition. Maybe we should think of 'Complaints' as a severity flag rather than a category? That way we can tag something as 'Claims Processing + Complaint' to show it's a problem that needs escalation.

I like the severity flag idea. From help desk, we see all of these categories depending on what the ticket is about. One thing I want to flag: some feedback is really just a question, not a complaint or suggestion. Should we have a 'Question/Clarification' category? Also, I'm wondering how we handle feedback that spans multiple categories—like a customer complains about delivery AND product quality.

From cellar visits, we mostly get 'Facility/Cellar Experience' and 'Product Quality' feedback. Some safety observations too. The checklist I'm designing will be simple—just a few questions about the tour experience. I think the taxonomy is fine for our purposes, but I want to make sure the tagging process doesn't require a lot of interpretation. Can we add some clear examples for edge cases?

Good feedback. Let me revise: I'll add 'Question/Clarification' as a category, and I'll restructure 'Complaints' as a severity flag that can be applied to any category. For multi-category feedback, we'll allow one primary tag and up to two secondary tags. I'll add more examples and edge cases to A2. I'll also create a simple routing matrix in A5 that shows: if feedback is tagged X, it goes to team Y with SLA Z. Let me work on that and post a revised version tomorrow.

That makes sense. One more thing: for routing, we need to be clear about escalation. If a complaint comes in about membership benefits, does it go to me first, or do we escalate to management? I want to make sure we're not creating bottlenecks.

Good point. The routing rules will include escalation thresholds. For example: standard feedback goes to the team owner, but if it's flagged as a complaint AND it's about a sensitive topic, it escalates to management. I'll define those rules in A5 and we can review them together. I'm aiming to have the final taxonomy and routing rules approved by end of week so we can move to scripts and training.
I'll review the revised taxonomy against our insurance complaint codes and send you a mapping by Thursday. That way we can make sure nothing falls through the cracks.
I'll test the revised categories on a sample of recent help desk tickets to make sure the tagging is intuitive. I'll send feedback by Friday.

Perfect. So here's the plan: I'll post the revised taxonomy and routing rules by tomorrow EOD. You all review and test by Friday. We'll do a quick sync call Friday afternoon to finalize and approve. Once we have D3 and D4 locked in, we can move to scripts and training. Sound good?

threads.thread_goal: Align on frontline scripts, checklists, and training approach.

messages.text: I've drafted a help desk intake script for capturing structured feedback. It covers greeting, consent, a brief data privacy notice, and then asks the customer to describe their feedback in their own words, followed by a few clarifying questions about category and urgency. I've tested it on 5 recent tickets and it adds about 2-3 minutes to the interaction, which feels manageable. The script is in A4. I'm also thinking about how to make this work for phone, email, and web forms—each channel might need a slight variation. What do you think?

The script looks good. For membership, I'm thinking we need something similar but lighter—we don't want to feel like we're interrogating members. I'm drafting a short survey that we can send via email after member events or renewals. It's just 3-4 questions: 'How was your experience?', 'What could we improve?', and 'Can we contact you about this feedback?'. I'll have that ready by tomorrow. For training, I think we need a short session for each team—maybe 30 minutes—to walk through the script and the taxonomy.

For cellar visits, I'm designing a simple one-page checklist that staff can use during tours. It has sections for tour experience, product feedback, and safety observations. The format is paper-based so it works during tours without needing a tablet or system access. I'll have a draft by tomorrow. For training, I'll need to walk the cellar team through how to use it and where to hand off the completed checklists to BI for logging.

Good. So we have three different collection methods: help desk script (structured intake), membership survey (email-based), and cellar checklist (paper-based). That makes sense given the different contexts. For training, I'm thinking we do one session per team next week—help desk Monday, membership Tuesday, cellar Wednesday. Each session covers the script/survey/checklist, the taxonomy, and how to tag and route feedback. I'll prepare training materials that walk through examples from each team's context.

One thing I want to make sure of: the script needs to include a clear data privacy statement. Customers need to know what we're doing with their feedback, how long we keep it, and who can see it. I'll coordinate with you on the exact wording so it's consistent across all channels.
I'll draft the privacy statement and send it to you both by tomorrow. It needs to cover data handling, retention, and access. Once we have that locked in, we can finalize the scripts.

Perfect. So here's the timeline: by end of tomorrow, we'll have the help desk script (with privacy statement), membership survey, and cellar checklist all drafted. We'll review and refine Friday, and then we're ready to sign off on D5 and D6. Once those are approved, we can schedule training sessions for next week.

I'll have the membership survey and communication plan ready by tomorrow EOD. I'm also thinking about how we announce this to members—we need to explain why we're collecting feedback and how it helps us improve. That's part of the customer communication plan.
Cellar checklist will be ready tomorrow. One question: when we hand off completed checklists to BI, what's the process? Do we scan them, enter them into a system, or just pass them along?

Good question. For the pilot, we'll keep it simple: you hand off the completed checklists to me at the end of each week, I'll log them into a shared sheet (A5) with the appropriate tags, and that feeds into the dashboard. Once we see how much volume we get, we can decide if we need to automate that process. For now, manual is fine.

Alright, I think we're aligned. By end of week we'll have all scripts and checklists finalized, privacy statement approved, and training materials ready. We'll do a final review Friday and then lock in D5 and D6. Training sessions start Monday. Does everyone feel good about this plan?

threads.thread_goal: Set up KPI tracking, data protection rules, and dashboard expectations.

messages.text: I've drafted a KPI framework for the pilot. I'm proposing we track: (1) Feedback volume by channel and category, (2) Average resolution time by category, (3) Escalation rate (how many feedback items get escalated), (4) Customer satisfaction with response (if we can capture it), and (5) Staff adoption rate (are teams actually using the process?). I've also drafted data protection rules in A7 that define who can access what data, retention periods, and anonymisation rules. The dashboard will pull from a shared feedback log (A5) and refresh daily. I want to make sure the KPIs are meaningful and the data handling is compliant. What are your thoughts?

The KPIs look reasonable. For data protection, I have some concerns about the access rules. Insurance complaints are sensitive—we need to make sure only authorized people can see them. I'm thinking we should have different access levels: BI can see everything for analysis, but team members only see feedback relevant to their team. Also, we need to define retention periods—how long do we keep the data after the pilot ends?

I agree on access levels. From help desk perspective, we don't need to see membership or insurance feedback—that's not our business. But we do need to see our own feedback and any feedback that's been routed to us. Also, customers are going to ask about privacy—we need to be able to tell them exactly what we do with their data. The privacy statement needs to be clear and honest.

Same from membership side. We need to know what feedback we're getting from members, but we don't need to see help desk or insurance data. And yes, we'll be telling members about this pilot, so the privacy statement is critical. I want to make sure we're being transparent about what we're collecting and why.

Got it. So the access model is: each team can see feedback relevant to their channel, BI can see everything for analysis and reporting, and we anonymise data where possible for the dashboard. For retention, I'm thinking we keep detailed feedback for 90 days after the pilot ends, then anonymise and archive. Does that work?
90 days works for insurance. I'll review the full data protection rules and send you feedback by tomorrow. I want to make sure we're compliant with any regulations around complaint data.

From cellar side, we're not collecting sensitive personal data—mostly just feedback about the tour experience. But I want to make sure we're not storing names or contact info longer than necessary. The checklist should be anonymised once it's logged into the system.

Good point. I'll update A7 to specify that cellar feedback is anonymised immediately upon logging. For the dashboard, I'll show volume and category mix, but no personal identifiers. I'll also add a note about the daily refresh—we'll update the dashboard every morning with the previous day's feedback. That way teams can see patterns emerging in real time.

One more thing: we need to document how we handle feedback that contains sensitive information—like if a customer mentions a health issue or financial problem. Should we flag that and handle it differently?

Good catch. I'll add a rule to A7: if feedback contains sensitive personal information, it gets flagged and only the relevant team can see it. BI can see that it exists and the category, but not the details. That way we protect privacy but still track volume. I'll have the updated A7 ready by tomorrow, and we can review and approve D7 and D8 by Friday.
I'll review the updated rules by Thursday and confirm they're compliant. Once we have D8 locked in, we can move forward with confidence.

Perfect. So by end of week we'll have the KPI framework and data protection rules finalized and approved. The dashboard will be ready to go live when the pilot starts next week. I'll also prepare a simple guide for how to read the dashboard and what the KPIs mean. Sound good?

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results and agree on next steps and roadmap.

messages.text: Alright team, we've completed the 4-week pilot and I've compiled the results. Here's what we learned: we captured 847 feedback items across all channels. Help desk contributed 42%, membership 28%, cellar visits 18%, and insurance 12%. The taxonomy worked well—most feedback fit cleanly into our categories. Resolution times averaged 3.2 days, which is reasonable. We had a 15% escalation rate, mostly for complaints about billing and claims processing. Staff adoption was solid—about 85% of interactions included structured feedback capture. I've drafted the evaluation report in A8 with detailed analysis and recommendations. The big question now is: do we extend this to all teams, scale it up, or iterate further before rolling out?

These numbers look good. From membership perspective, we got valuable feedback about event experiences and membership benefits. The 28% of total volume is higher than I expected, which tells me members are engaged. One thing I noticed: we got a lot of suggestions for new events and benefits. That's useful input for our planning. I think we should extend this process—it's working.

From help desk side, the script worked well. Customers didn't seem to mind the extra 2-3 minutes, and we got much better structured feedback than before. The 42% volume makes sense—we're the main entry point for customer contact. One challenge: we had some feedback that didn't fit neatly into the taxonomy, so we had to use 'Other' more than I'd like. Maybe we need to refine the categories based on what we learned?

Cellar visits went smoothly. The checklist was easy to use and didn't disrupt the tour experience. We got good feedback about the facility and product. The 18% volume is reasonable given we only collect during tours. One thing: we had some feedback about staff knowledge and tour quality that was valuable. I think this process should continue.

Insurance side: the 12% volume is lower than I expected, but that might be because we're only capturing new complaints through the new process. We didn't retroactively tag existing complaints. The mapping between our codes and the new taxonomy worked well. I think we should extend this, but we need to make sure we're capturing all complaints, not just new ones.

Good point. The 12% might be artificially low because we didn't backfill historical data. For the next phase, we should include all complaints, not just new ones. That will give us a more complete picture. Overall, I think the pilot was successful. We proved the concept works, teams adopted it, and we got valuable insights. I'm recommending we move to a 'scale' phase: extend the process to all teams, refine the taxonomy based on feedback, and set up permanent KPI tracking.

I agree with scaling. But I want to make sure we have the resources to support it. Training was manageable for the pilot, but if we're rolling out to more teams, we need a plan for that. Also, we should think about how to use the insights we're getting—are we actually making changes based on the feedback?

Good question. From help desk perspective, we've already made some changes based on pilot feedback—we clarified some of our response templates and improved our escalation process. But we need a formal process for reviewing feedback regularly and deciding what to act on. That should be part of the next phase.

Absolutely. I'm recommending we set up a monthly feedback review meeting where each team presents insights and we decide on actions. That way the feedback loop is closed and customers see that we're actually listening. I've included that in the recommendations in A8. So here's my proposal: we extend the process to all teams, refine the taxonomy, set up monthly reviews, and plan for a full rollout in Q2. Does that work for everyone?

I'm on board with extending and scaling. One thing I want to flag: we need to make sure the data protection rules scale with the volume. As we get more feedback, we need to be even more careful about privacy and compliance. I'll review the rules and make sure they hold up at scale.

From cellar side, I'm ready to continue. The process works well and doesn't disrupt operations. I'll keep collecting feedback and passing it along to BI. If we're scaling, I might need to think about how to handle feedback during peak season, but for now it's manageable.

Perfect. So we're aligned: extend the pilot to all teams, refine based on what we learned, set up monthly reviews, and plan for Q2 rollout. I'll finalize the evaluation report and recommendations in A8 and share it with leadership for approval. This has been a great pilot—thanks everyone for your effort and collaboration. The feedback process is now part of how we operate.
